source.title: How feature learning can improve neural scaling laws
source.authors: Blake Bordelon; Alexander Atanasov; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.file_problem: Whole paper is present. Some equations and figure labels show minor text-extraction artifacts, but the main text and relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study develops and tests a feature-learning scaling model that refines when power-law exponents and compute-optimal scaling apply. It reports task-dependent exponents and a nonlinear-network curve that eventually departs from the predicted power law.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own scaling results for a theoretical model, nonlinear MLPs, vision CNNs, linear networks, and a transformer. Cited results from earlier work are not recorded as rows. The transformer test is a single training-time/token curve, not a sweep over model size or compute. No downstream-task results or architecture-shape comparison are reported.
record.test_reason: A solvable model plus experiments (MLPs, CNNs on MNIST-1M and CIFAR-5M, linear nets, one C4 transformer) show that loss-vs-time exponents, and so compute-optimal trade-offs, depend on task spectrum (β) and feature-learning strength (γ). That is an argument and evidence bearing on V7. The vision and synthetic runs also report power laws outside text pretraining (V5). The single transformer gives a power-law token curve (V1, tokens only).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points the paraphrase omits. Feature learning nearly doubles the time exponent for hard (out-of-RKHS) tasks, which changes the compute-optimal N/t strategy. Easy and super-easy tasks keep lazy exponents. A single transformer test roughly shows exponent doubling despite cross-entropy loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a projected-SGD feature-learning model and tests it with task-spectrum experiments; it does not reproduce the original language-model scaling experiments. Its main theory uses MSE, and its transformer experiment is a limited cross-entropy training-time test.
record.method_sensitivity: The exponent depends on task difficulty/source exponent β and differs between lazy and feature-learning regimes. The paper also reports a late-training change on CIFAR-5M and varying outcomes with feature-learning strength γ or γ₀.

fits_no_version.finding: For hard tasks, SGD batch noise does not alter the scaling exponent; in super-easy tasks it does (Fig 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minibatch noise affects scaling exponents only for tasks inside the initial kernel's RKHS.

record.problems: The main solvable theory is for MSE with SGD and features restricted to combinations of initial features; the authors identify these as limitations for modern models. The CNN and transformer values are principally figure-based, without tabulated fit errors. The transformer experiment is a single setup, and CIFAR-5M departs from the predicted exponent after sufficient training.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant outcomes were omitted. Per-γ curves and individual plotted MLP cases were not split into separate rows where the text reports only an aggregate conclusion; Figures 2–5 and 12 contain the associated plots.

untested.parts: Scaling with parameters or compute for LMs; multi-model sweeps; only one small transformer vs tokens.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All for LMs: toy-model compute-optimal loss exponents only, no LM N/D allocation exponents.
Fine-tuning/transfer; empirical repeated-data runs; image/video generative models.

missing.what: For a fixed target, changing the activation exponent qϕ changes the measured loss-time exponent in MLPs
Finite-N toy curves saturate at the N^-αβ model bottleneck, with sims matching theory
Easy-task MLPs where feature learning does not alter long-time scaling

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Theory rows R1–R6 are toy-model derivations, not LMs, so they are linked only to V7/V5 as argument, not to V3. Empirical values are figure-based with no tabulated fit errors.

versions.untested_parts: The language-model experiment tests cross-entropy loss against training time/tokens for one transformer setup; it does not test scaling with parameter count or compute, or a multi-model sweep.
No experiment fits power laws on smaller runs and tests predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.

Compute-optimal loss exponents and trade-offs are analyzed for the study's model and task regimes, but it does not establish parameter- and token-count growth exponents for language models or compare the Kaplan and Hoffmann empirical setups.
No controlled comparison varies depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The study tests synthetic function fitting, vision tasks, and one next-token transformer experiment; it does not test fine-tuning or transfer, and its repeated-data result is theoretical rather than a reported repeated-data network experiment.
No downstream-task performance is measured or predicted.

The study examines task difficulty, feature-learning strength, and a late curve departure, but does not compare parameter-counting conventions, alternative fitting methods, or training schedules as sources of published-exponent disagreement.

rows.subject: two-layer linear model with projected SGD
rows.operation_detail: Derives loss scaling with training time and model size under power-law feature and target spectra.
rows.measure: Test loss versus training time in the infinite-size, infinite-batch limit
rows.value: Feature-learning time exponent χ = 2β/(1+β); loss scales as t^-χ. The model-bottleneck term is N^-αβ.
rows.note: The exponent improvement is derived for hard tasks in the study's model; the paper says the finite-N simulations agree with its theory.
rows.check: Toy-model theory, not an LM, so drop V3. It gives compute-optimal loss exponents, not N/t allocation exponents. For V7 it shows feature learning raises the hard-task exponent from β to 2β/(1+β).

rows.subject: two-layer linear model with projected SGD
rows.operation_detail: Derives time, finite-model, and compute-optimal loss scaling for tasks within the initial kernel RKHS.
rows.measure: Loss scaling with training time, model size, and compute
rows.value: The time exponent remains β; the finite-model transient is N^-1 t^-(1-1/α); the compute-optimal loss exponent is αβ/(αβ+1).
rows.locator: Sections 4 and compute-optimal scaling discussion; Table 1; Figure 4(b)
rows.note: The study reports that feature learning does not change the asymptotic time exponent for easy tasks.
rows.check: Drop V3 (toy theory, loss exponent only). For easy tasks the exponent depends on α,β but not on lazy vs rich, so the setup-dependence is only partial.

rows.subject: two-layer linear model with projected SGD
rows.operation_detail: Derives compute-optimal loss scaling for very easy tasks, including finite-batch SGD effects.
rows.value: The large-compute loss exponent is 1 - 1/(2α), obtained by balancing the finite-N transient and SGD-noise terms.
rows.locator: Table 1; Sections 4 and compute-optimal scaling discussion; Figure 4(c)
rows.note: This is a task-regime-specific compute-optimal result, rather than a universal allocation exponent.
rows.check: Drop V3. The super-easy regime has a different compute exponent, set by SGD noise and finite N, so it is regime-dependent.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, compute-optimal scaling discussion; Table 1; Figure 4(c).

rows.subject: two-layer linear model with projected SGD
rows.operation_detail: Derives the lazy-limit reference scaling and compares it with feature-learning scaling.
rows.value: The lazy-limit loss scales as t^-β; the compute-optimal loss exponent is αβ/(α+1).
rows.note: The lazy result is the study's comparison condition for its rich-regime analysis.
rows.check: Lazy comparator (exponent αβ/(α+1)). Its value is a derived reference, not a weak effect, so 'partial' was wrong. Against R1 it shows the regime changes the hard-task exponent. Drop V3.

rows.subject: two-layer linear model with projected SGD
rows.operation_detail: Derives the lazy-limit compute-optimal loss scaling for easy tasks.
rows.value: The compute-optimal loss exponent is αβ/(αβ+1), the same as in the rich regime for easy tasks.
rows.note: The paper states that the easy-task compute exponent is unchanged from the lazy model.
rows.check: Drop V3. For easy tasks the lazy and rich compute exponents are identical, so the regime choice does not matter here.

rows.subject: two-layer linear model with projected SGD
rows.operation_detail: Derives test-loss scaling when training examples are reused.
rows.measure: Asymptotic test loss versus dataset size
rows.baseline: Lazy-limit dataset-size exponent is not separately stated here
rows.note: This is a theoretical data-reuse result, not a reported empirical repeated-data network run.
rows.check: Theoretical derivation for repeated data in the toy model (P^-α min{2,β}, same as lazy), not an empirical network run.

rows.subject: depth-4, width-512 nonlinear MLPs
rows.operation_detail: Trains nonlinear MLPs on power-law Fourier target functions on the circle and compares loss curves with predicted exponents.

conditions.value: varying β, including β < 1 and β > 1

rows.value: The authors report that the predicted feature-learning exponent t^-β max{1, 2/(1+β)} provides a very accurate prediction across the tested cases.
rows.note: The figure aggregates multiple tested β values; the text describes the overall agreement but does not give per-condition numerical fit errors.
rows.check: Aggregates Fig 5(a), 5(b) and 7(b). Fig 5(b) shows activation (qϕ) changes the exponent for a fixed target; it is not split out.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1, equations 13–14; Figure 5(a); Appendix A.1 and Figure 7(b).

rows.subject: CNNs on MNIST-1M
rows.operation_detail: Measures test loss across training time and compares it with the predicted feature-learning power law.
rows.value: The text says the MNIST-1M scaling is very well captured by the predicted exponent.
rows.note: The paper describes the agreement in text; plotted values are not tabulated.
rows.check: Baseline should be the lazy t^-β curve. t^-2β/(1+β) is the prediction being tested, not the baseline.

rows.subject: CNNs on CIFAR-5M
rows.size_stated: same deep residual architecture as Bordelon et al. (2024a); width not stated here
rows.operation_detail: Measures test loss over training and compares its slope with the predicted feature-learning power law.
rows.value: The curve is initially described by the predicted exponent, then reaches a regime with a larger exponent than predicted after sufficient training.
rows.note: The authors explicitly identify a late-training departure from their prediction; per-time numerical values are not tabulated.
rows.check: For V5 the curve remains power-law-like, moving to a 'better power law'. For V7 this is a bend away from a single exponent. 'Partial' wrongly reflected the mismatch with the authors' own model, not with either version.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2; Figure 6(b); Section 6; Appendix A.2 and Figure 8.

rows.subject: depth-4 decoder-only transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compares cross-entropy loss against training tokens for lazy and feature-learning settings.

conditions.value: 10^-4 for lazy fit; 0.1 for feature-learning simulation

rows.baseline: Lazy curve fit to t^-β over 10^6 to 3 × 10^9 tokens
rows.value: The feature-learning curve is described as having roughly twice the exponent of the lazy curve; the new predicted exponent fits the data somewhat well at early times.
rows.note: The figure does not tabulate the exponent. This is one transformer setup and does not vary parameter count or compute.
rows.check: Not V5, since it is text pretraining. For V1, the lazy curve is fit as a power law over 10^6–3×10^9 tokens, single small model, no fit error reported. For V7, the exponent roughly doubles at large γ; the prediction fits 'somewhat well at early times'.

rows.subject: two-layer linear networks
rows.operation_detail: Compares loss scaling for easy and hard power-law tasks across feature-learning strengths.
rows.value: Feature-learning networks are reported to achieve the improved t^-2β/(1+β) scaling.
rows.note: The text explicitly states the improved rate; individual curve values are not tabulated.

rows.subject: two-layer linear networks
rows.operation_detail: Compares loss scaling across feature-learning strengths on an easy task.
rows.value: The text reports the same asymptotic t^-β scaling across γ values; larger γ can improve the loss by a multiplicative factor without changing the exponent.
rows.locator: Appendix G.2; Figure 12(a); Appendix G.3; Figure 13(a)
rows.note: The paper reports that the easy-task feature-learning spike plateaus rather than growing without bound.
rows.check: Power-law form is observed (V5). For V7, γ leaves the exponent unchanged on the easy task, so dependence holds only through β.

source_check.correct: Use version-specific states: observed for V5, partial for V7. The power-law form is observed across γ; feature learning changes the prefactor but leaves the easy-task exponent unchanged.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state understates the fully observed power-law form for V5.
